title: The alphabet psalm (Psalm 118 [119])
hookLine: 176 verses in 22 stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, all about God's word

cards: Maybe you learned the alphabet with a song. A is for apple, B is for ball, all the way to Z. Children love it because it has an order: you always know where you are and how far is left.
Now imagine someone doing that with a prayer. Every letter of their alphabet, in order, eight lines for each. Twenty-two letters.
A hundred seventy-six verses. The longest psalm in the Bible, and the longest chapter too.

teach.b: First, the shape. In Hebrew, this psalm is an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav.

All eight lines of the first stanza begin with aleph, every line of the second with beth, and so on to the end. Open a Douay-Rheims and you'll still see the letters printed as little headings: ALEPH, BETH, GHIMEL.
English can't keep the trick, but it keeps the signposts. Second, the subject.

All hundred seventy-six verses are about one thing: God's word. The poet keeps finding new names for it: law, testimonies, ways, precepts, commandments, justifications, words. Nearly every verse has one.
It opens: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord." Third, the feeling. You might expect a psalm about law to sound like a rulebook.

teach.h: NOT A RULEBOOK. A LOVE LETTER.
teach.b: It sounds like a love letter. Halfway through, the poet says: "O how have I loved thy law, O Lord! it is my meditation all the day." For the psalmist, God's law isn't a fence.
It's a gift, the way God has shown himself. Why an alphabet? Nobody knows for certain.
Some say it helped people memorize it.
Some say it's a way of saying everything, from A to Z, the whole of life, belongs to this love.

teach.h: O HOW HAVE I LOVED THY LAW, O LORD!
teach.b: Jews pray it, and so do Catholics: for centuries monks and priests prayed pieces of it every day in the Divine Office, a stanza or two at a time.

how: Catholics pray portions of Psalm 118 [119] in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hours, usually one stanza at a time, and some read one stanza a day as lectio divina.

games.q: you're the psalmist writing a hundred seventy-six verses about God's word. how do you keep it from repeating one dull term?
o: use the word law every time.
keep finding new names: testimonies, ways, precepts, words.
games.why: the poet keeps finding new names for God's word, and nearly every verse holds one of them.

practice: If you have a Bible nearby, read the first eight verses, the aleph stanza, slowly, out loud or in your head; if not, repeat its opening line: blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.
Notice which word catches you, and stay with that one.

wordCard.voice: Aleph. The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, opening the first stanza of the longest psalm: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter, all about God's word. Today's word.
